name: Eye-area radiofrequency / Thermage eyes

lead: Eye-area radiofrequency, often called Thermage eyes after the Solta Medical device, aims to tighten loose eyelid skin and soften wrinkles around the eyes without surgery. People want a smoother, lifted, less hooded look.

RF energy heats the dermis, with a target around 67 C described, which prompts collagen and elastin remodeling so the skin firms over the following months. Sources describe the technique in general and list one registered trial of an electrosurgical device for wrinkles at the eye corners.

paras: It is done by a clinician in a short office session using a handheld device, often as a single treatment or a short series, with tightening developing gradually over weeks to months. People often combine it with other eye-area treatments and skincare.

Reported problems include pain severe enough to need sedation, skin dents from uneven healing, fat necrosis and atrophic scarring. The eye area is delicate and no eye-specific safety data were described in the sources reviewed. Choosing an experienced provider is the common precaution.

angle.text: Users seek radiofrequency treatments such as Thermage eyes to tighten loose eyelid skin and soften wrinkles without surgery. RF heats the deeper skin, collagen remodels and tightens, and the eye area looks smoother and more lifted. One registered trial of a device for eye-corner wrinkles exists.

lead: Eye-area radiofrequency treatment, often called Thermage eyes after the Thermage device brand, applies RF energy to the skin around the eyes to tighten loose skin and reduce wrinkles. It is marketed as a noninvasive alternative to surgery [1].

RF skin tightening is described as heating the dermis to stimulate collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid production [1]. Many manufacturers make such devices, including Solta Medical (Thermage), Venus Concept, Syneron, BTL and Lumenis [1].
Evidence specific to the eye area is limited in the sources reviewed: a single registered device trial exists [2].

paras: RF devices use monopolar, bipolar or unipolar electrodes, which change how deep the energy penetrates [1]. Cited studies in the general literature include a blinded comparison of fractional RF with surgical facelift and studies showing new collagen and elastin formation, though several statements in the Wikipedia article carry citation-needed tags [1].
Wikipedia notes patients may report pain needing sedation, that improper application can leave dents from uneven healing, and that fat necrosis and atrophic scarring have been reported [1].

A registered single-blind, paired-design, non-inferiority device trial (n=80, completed, started 2024) assessed a universal electrosurgical device for temporary improvement of mild and moderate wrinkles around the eye corners and cheek folds [2]. No results were available for this article, so no efficacy conclusions are given.
